aspects.says: get(timeout, unit) on a submitted task bounds the wait, reports failures in an ExecutionException, and shutdownNow interrupts a task still running.
The common pool's parallelism defaults to availableProcessors() - 1 and can be set with -Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism.
aspects.reason: a JVM setting whose value depends on the machine and container the tests run on, so a graded answer cannot be checked against it

aspects.says: The common pool is shared by parallel streams and CompletableFuture, so blocking calls in it slow every user in the JVM.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: Fork/Join suits CPU-bound decomposition, while I/O-bound concurrency is better served by virtual threads.
aspects.reason: a design choice between tools that no test can grade; it is asked in the overview page's quiz

aspects.says: A custom ForkJoinPool with its own parallelism isolates work from the JVM-wide common pool.
execute(task) returns nothing, and a failure is seen only by keeping the task and calling join() or get() on it.
invoke(task) blocks until the task completes, returns its result and rethrows its exception to the caller.
A blocking call inside a pool is wrapped in a ManagedBlocker and run through ForkJoinPool.managedBlock, so the pool can compensate with another thread.
A ForkJoinPool can also be given a thread factory, an uncaught exception handler and asyncMode for FIFO processing.
aspects.reason: constructor options listed for reference; the page gives no task that needs them, so a practice would only repeat the constructor call

aspects.says: The pool size can grow beyond the parallelism while ManagedBlocker compensates for a blocked worker.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: A custom pool is shut down in a finally block, so it releases its threads even when the task fails.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: A parallel stream submitted as a task to a custom pool runs its work in that pool.
aspects.reason: practised on the overview page 6.6.1 by its stream-in-pool practice, which its own Q5 teaches; not drafted twice

aspects.says: submit(task) returns a ForkJoinTask future at once, so several tasks can be submitted before any is joined.
Null, empty and single-element inputs are handled before anything is submitted to the pool.
aspects.reason: a minor guard with nothing further to practise; the RecursiveTask practices of page 6.6.1.2 cover the base case of a small range

aspects.says: Each worker has its own deque, and an idle worker steals a forked task from the other end of a busy worker's deque.
aspects.reason: which worker steals which task is up to the scheduler, so no test can observe it deterministically; it is asked in the quiz of page 6.6.1.4, which explains the deque ends
